o: For each (student_id, subject) pair we need the score on the earliest exam date and the score on the latest exam date. A pair qualifies only if it has at least two distinct exam dates and latest_score > first_score; ties on dates are impossible since (student_id, subject, exam_date) is the primary key. In the example, student 101 qualifies for Math (70 → 85) but not Physics (65 → 60), student 103 is excluded because Math was taken only once, and students 102 and 104 qualify. The constraints imply a simple grouping/aggregation over the table: group by (student_id, subject), pick scores at min/max exam_date, filter, and sort.
k: Group by (student_id, subject); the first/latest score is the score at MIN(exam_date)/MAX(exam_date).
Window functions let you fetch both boundary scores in one pass without self-joins.
The 'at least two different dates' condition is automatically satisfied when first_score < latest_score, but must be checked explicitly otherwise.

a.i: Join the Scores table to itself on (student_id, subject) so every row pairs with every other row of the same student-subject. For each group, take the score of the row with the minimum exam_date as first_score and the maximum exam_date as latest_score, then keep groups where they differ and latest > first. This directly mirrors the problem definition and works in any SQL dialect.
s: Self-join Scores s1 with Scores s2 on student_id and subject.
Group by s1.student_id, s1.subject, s1.exam_date to anchor the 'first' attempt.
first_score = s1.score where s1.exam_date = MIN date of the group; latest_score = MAX(s2.score at max date).
Filter HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 (at least two dates) AND latest_score > first_score.

c.python:
# Database problem — solution expressed as MySQL query:
SELECT
    s1.student_id,
    s1.subject,
    s1.score AS first_score,
    MAX(CASE WHEN s2.exam_date = t.mx THEN s2.score END) AS latest_score
FROM Scores s1
JOIN Scores s2
  ON s1.student_id = s2.student_id AND s1.subject = s2.subject
JOIN (
    SELECT student_id, subject, MIN(exam_date) AS mn, MAX(exam_date) AS mx
    FROM Scores GROUP BY student_id, subject
) t ON t.student_id = s1.student_id AND t.subject = s1.subject
WHERE s1.exam_date = t.mn
GROUP BY s1.student_id, s1.subject, s1.exam_date, s1.score, t.mx
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT s2.exam_date) > 1
   AND MAX(CASE WHEN s2.exam_date = t.mx THEN s2.score END) > s1.score
ORDER BY s1.student_id, s1.subject;

a.t: O(n^2) in the worst case due to the self-join producing all pairs within each (student, subject) group before aggregation.
a.sp: O(n) extra space for the join results and grouped aggregates.

a.i: Use FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE (or ROW_NUMBER against min/max dates) partitioned by (student_id, subject) ordered by exam_date to attach the first and latest scores to every row in a single pass. Then DISTINCT the needed columns and filter where first < latest, which also guarantees at least two rows exist. This avoids any join and is the idiomatic modern-SQL answer.
s: In a CTE, compute FIRST_VALUE(score) OVER (PARTITION BY student_id, subject ORDER BY exam_date) as first_score.
Compute LAST_VALUE(score) OVER (PARTITION BY student_id, subject ORDER BY exam_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) as latest_score.
Select DISTINCT student_id, subject, first_score, latest_score from the CTE.
Filter WHERE latest_score > first_score (this implies >= 2 exams).

c.python:
# Database problem — MySQL 8+ window-function solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        student_id,
        subject,
        FIRST_VALUE(score) OVER w AS first_score,
        LAST_VALUE(score) OVER w AS latest_score
    FROM Scores
    WINDOW w AS (
        PARTITION BY student_id, subject
        ORDER BY exam_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    )
)
SELECT DISTINCT student_id, subject, first_score, latest_score
FROM ranked
WHERE latest_score > first_score
ORDER BY student_id, subject;

a.t: O(n log n) — one sort per window partition by (student_id, subject, exam_date), then a linear scan.
a.sp: O(n) for the windowed intermediate result.

w: Prefer Approach 2 in an interview: it's a single pass, needs no joins, and shows fluency with window functions; mention Approach 1 as a fallback for older databases lacking window support. Common pitfalls: forgetting that LAST_VALUE defaults to the current row's frame (must specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING), using MAX(score) instead of the score at the latest date (they differ when the best score isn't the last one), and skipping the DISTINCT which would duplicate output rows once per exam taken. Edge cases: single-exam subjects (excluded automatically since first_score = latest_score fails strict inequality), equal first and latest scores (not an improvement), and date ordering — exam_date sorts lexicographically correctly in ISO format. Follow-ups: return students improved in *all* subjects, or the largest per-student improvement amount.
